summary.text: 友 is formed from two hand forms, 又, traditionally associated with friendship. The two forms may also contribute a sound cue, though their individual roles are unresolved.

formation.text: The graph is analyzed as a semantic compound of two hands, or as a phono-semantic compound in which 又 also provides sound. The proposed phonetic role is plausible, but evidence does not determine whether one or both repeated forms supply it.

components.text: 又 depicts a hand. Here the two 又 forms are described as facing the same way and sometimes joined, supporting an interpretation in which the hands contribute the idea of friendship. CUHK also assigns 又 a phonetic role, but the function of each repeated form is unresolved.

sound_limitation.text: The historical comparisons make a phonetic contribution plausible but do not establish whether one or both repeated 又 forms provide it. The modern Mandarin resemblance alone does not establish an ancient sound role.

sound.text: The modern Mandarin readings are similar, but that resemblance alone does not establish an ancient sound relationship.
The Middle Chinese readings share the same initial and rhyme notation but differ in tone category.
In this reconstruction, the forms share initial and most rhyme material but differ in the final element, making a phonetic connection plausible without establishing the component’s role.
In this system, the forms share initial and medial/rime material but differ in the final element.

history.text: Oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and small-seal forms are reported. Early forms are described as two similarly oriented hands, sometimes joined; in small seal, the forms are arranged vertically. This records a change in layout without establishing a particular cooperative scene.
The received Shuowen explanation links the two 又 forms with people who share aims and interact as friends. This is a traditional interpretation of the graph.

uncertainties.text: Accounts differ on whether the two 又 forms contribute meaning alone or also sound. Sound comparisons support a possible phonetic role but do not determine which repeated form has which function.

The earliest reported contexts include a personal name and a sacrificial use read as 侑. The evidence does not establish “friend” as the earliest attested sense or a continuous path from those uses to later friend and associate uses.
A Mawangdui manuscript is reported to use 友 to write 柔, “soft.” This is a separate use of the whole graph for another word; the sound basis for the borrowing is not established here.

senses.period: oracle-bone context; absolute dating of the cited witness unresolved
senses.text: The graph is reported in use as a personal name. This attestation does not establish its original meaning.

senses.text: The graph is also reported in a sacrificial context, read as 侑, “assist in sacrifice.” Its priority relative to the personal-name use is unresolved.

senses.period: Western Zhou bronze contexts reported; individual witness dates unresolved
senses.text: Bronze inscriptions are reported using 友 for friend or friendly relations and for associates. These uses do not establish a semantic development from the reported name or sacrificial use.
A dictionary records a verb meaning to make friends or become acquainted; the supplied example does not date this use.
“Love” is listed as a use, with no supplied chronology or supported link to other senses.
Assistance or cooperation is listed as a use, with no supplied chronology or supported link to other senses.
友 is used for a friend or companion.

limitations.text: The attested uses do not establish a chronological or semantic bridge among the early name, sacrificial, friend, associate, verbal, and other listed uses; no development between them is asserted.
The reported 友-for-柔 manuscript spelling is borrowing of the graph for another word, not a demonstrated development in the meaning of 友. The sound basis for the borrowing is not established here.

overview.text: 友 combines two forms identified as hands (又), traditionally linked with friendship. It means “friend” or “companion”; accounts differ on whether the hands also cue its sound.

components.text: 又 depicts a hand. The two forms are linked with friendship; whether they also cue the sound remains unsettled.

relationships.text: The two 又 forms are interpreted as hands contributing the idea of friendship, though the intended scene is uncertain.
Each 又 is identified as a hand form, and the graph brings two such forms together. This describes the imagery without asserting a literal scene of cooperation.

One account explicitly assigns 又 a sound role. Old Chinese comparisons show similar forms with a differing final element, but do not establish whether one or both repeated 又 forms supply the sound cue.
